en: Majjhima Nikāya 125,
Dantabhūmisutta:
Thus have I heard.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time the novice Aciravata was dwelling in a forest hut.
Then Prince Jayasena, while walking and wandering for exercise, approached the novice Aciravata; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the novice Aciravata.
Having exchanged greetings and pleasantries, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Prince Jayasena said to the novice Aciravata:
"I have heard this, Master Aggivessana:
'Here, a bhikkhu dwelling diligent, ardent, and resolute may attain one-pointedness of mind.'"
“It is so, prince; it is so, prince.
Here, a bhikkhu dwelling diligent, ardent, and resolute might attain one-pointedness of mind.
“Venerable Aggivessana, please teach me the Dhamma as you have heard it and mastered it.”
“I am not able, prince, to teach you the Dhamma exactly as I have heard it and mastered it.
For if I were to teach you the Dhamma exactly as I have heard it and mastered it, you might not understand the meaning of what I say; that would be weariness for me, that would be a vexation for me.
“May the venerable Aggivessana teach me the Dhamma exactly as he has heard it and mastered it.”
“Perhaps I might understand the meaning of what has been said by the venerable Aggivessana.
“I would indeed teach you the Dhamma, prince, as I have heard it and as I have mastered it.
If you could understand the meaning of what I say, that would be well.”
“If you do not understand the meaning of what I have said, you should remain as you are and not question me further on that matter.
“May the venerable Aggivessana teach me the Dhamma as he has heard it and as he has mastered it.
If I understand the meaning of the venerable Aggivessana’s words, that will be well.”
“If I do not understand the meaning of what the venerable Aggivessana has said, I shall remain as I am and will not question the venerable Aggivessana further on that matter.
Then the novice Aciravata taught the Dhamma to Prince Jayasena exactly as he had heard it and mastered it.
When this was said, Prince Jayasena spoke thus to the novice Aciravata:
“It is impossible, Master Aggivessana, it is out of the question that a bhikkhu who dwells heedful, ardent, and resolute could attain one-pointedness of mind.
Then Prince Jayasena, having declared to the novice Aciravata both the impossibility and the out-of-the-question nature of this, rose from his seat and departed.
Not long after Prince Jayasena had left, the novice Aciravata approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Sitting to one side, the novice Aciravata reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation he had had with Prince Jayasena.
When this was said, the Blessed One addressed the novice Aciravata:
"How could that be possible here, Aggivessana?"
That which is to be known through renunciation, seen through renunciation, attained through renunciation,
and realized through renunciation— that indeed Prince Jayasena, living in the midst of sensual pleasures, enjoying sensual pleasures,
being devoured by thoughts of sensual pleasure, burning with the fever of sensual pleasure, and eager for the pursuit of sensual pleasure, will surely come to know.
or will see it, or will realize it for himself—this is impossible.

It is just as if, Aggivessana, there were two well-trained and well-disciplined elephant-tamers, horse-tamers, or ox-tamers, and two untrained and undisciplined elephant-tamers, horse-tamers, or ox-tamers.
What do you think, Aggivessana?

“Those two elephant-tamers, or horse-tamers, or ox-tamers who have well-tamed and well-trained [animals]—would those tamed ones go for the purpose of being tamed, and would they reach the stage of being tamed?
“Yes, venerable sir.
“But as for those two elephant-tamers, or horse-tamers, or ox-tamers who have not tamed and have not trained [the animals], would those...”
“Would those who are untamed go to the place for taming, and would those who are untamed reach the ground of the tamed,
just as those two well-tamed and well-trained elephant-keepers, horse-keepers, or cow-keepers [would do]?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“In the same way, Aggivessana, that which is to be known through renunciation, seen through renunciation, attained through renunciation,
and realized through renunciation— that, indeed, Prince Jayasena, while living in the midst of sensual pleasures, enjoying sensual pleasures,
being devoured by thoughts of sensual pleasure, burning with the fever of sensual pleasure, and seeking after sensual pleasures— ”
‘One who is eager will know it, see it, or realize it’— this is impossible. Aggivessana,
it is just as if there were a great mountain not far from a village or town,
and two friends, having departed from that village or town, were to cross it by leaping hand over hand.
Suppose they were to approach that mountain; having approached, one companion would stand at the foot of the mountain while the other companion would climb to the top of the mountain.
Then, the companion standing at the foot of the mountain would say to the companion standing on the top of the mountain:
“‘Friend, what do you see when standing on the upper mountain?
He would say:
‘Standing on the upper mountain, friend, I see delightful parks, delightful groves, delightful landscapes, and delightful lotus ponds.’”
Then one might say:

"It is impossible, my friend, it is out of the question that while you are standing on the upper mountain, you could see the delightful parks, the delightful groves, the delightful landscapes, and the delightful lotus ponds.

Then a companion, standing on the upper mountain, having descended to the foot of the lower mountain, would take his friend by the arm, lead him up to the upper mountain, give him a moment's rest, and say this:
“‘Friend, standing on the upper mountain, what do you see?
He would say:
‘Standing on the upper mountain, friend, I see delightful parks, delightful groves, delightful landscapes, and delightful lotus ponds.’”
Then one might say:
“Just now, my friend, you said: ‘We understand it thus:
it is impossible, my friend, it cannot happen that while standing on a high mountain you would see delightful parks, delightful groves, delightful landscapes, and delightful lotus ponds.’”
And just now, we understood your speech thus:
"Friend, standing on the upper mountain, I see delightful parks, delightful groves, delightful landscapes, and delightful lotus ponds.
He might then say:
“Because, friend, being enclosed by this great mountain, Prince Jayasena could not see what was worth seeing.
“Even greater than that, Aggivessana, is Prince Jayasena enclosed, shut in, covered, and enveloped by the mass of ignorance.
Indeed, that which is to be known through renunciation, to be seen through renunciation, and to be attained through renunciation—”
‘That Prince Jayasena, living in the midst of sensual pleasures, enjoying sensual pleasures, being devoured by thoughts of sensual pleasure,
burning with the fever of sensual pleasure, and eager in the pursuit of sensual pleasure, should know, see,
or realize that which is to be realized through renunciation— that is impossible.’”

“If, Aggivessana, these two similes were to occur to you regarding Prince Jayasena, it would not be surprising if Prince Jayasena were to place his confidence in you, and being confident, were to show you that he is confident.
“But from where, Bhante, would these two similes occur to me regarding Prince Jayasena—similes that are marvelous and unheard of before, just as they have been heard by the Blessed One?
“Aggivessana, it is just as if a head-anointed Kṣatriya king were to address an elephant trainer:”
‘Come, friend elephant-keeper, mount the king’s elephant, enter the elephant forest, and having overtaken the wild elephant, tether him to the neck of the king’s elephant.
‘Very well, sire,’ Aggivessana, the elephant-keeper replied to the consecrated kṣatriya king.
Having mounted the king’s elephant and entered the elephant forest, he overtook the wild elephant and tethered it to the neck of the king’s elephant.
They bind it by the neck.
Then the king’s elephant leads it out into the open air.
It is in this way, Aggivessana, that a forest elephant has gone out into the open air.
For it is here, Aggivessana, that the wild elephants have their attachment, namely, the elephant forest.
Then the keeper of the elephant forest would inform the anointed Kṣatriya king:
"Sire, the wild elephant has come out into the open."
Then, Aggivessana, the anointed khattiya king addressed that elephant trainer:
"Come, friend elephant trainer, tame this forest elephant for the purpose of crushing its wild habits,
for the purpose of crushing its wild intentions and resolves, and for the purpose of crushing its wild distress, fatigue, and fever."
‘To utterly subdue him, to make him take delight in the village, and to establish him in the virtues dear to human beings.
‘Very well, Your Majesty,’ the elephant trainer replied to the anointed Khattiya king.
Having done so, he dug a large post into the ground and bound the wild elephant’s neck to it.
It is for the crushing of forest-dwelling virtues, for the crushing of forest-dwelling intentions,
for the crushing of forest-dwelling distress, fatigue, and fever, for delighting in the vicinity of villages,
and for establishing others in the virtues dear to human beings.
Then the elephant trainer addresses him with speech that is gentle, pleasing to the ear, affectionate, heart-moving, urbane, agreeable to many people,
and dear to many people. When, Aggivessana, the forest elephant is thus addressed by the elephant trainer with such speech— speech that is gentle, pleasing to the ear, affectionate,
heart-moving, urbane, agreeable to many people, and dear to many people—
He desires to hear, he lends an ear, and he applies his mind to understanding;
then the elephant-tamer provides him with further grass, fodder, and water.
Aggivessana, when the forest elephant accepts the grass, fodder, and water from the elephant-tamer, it occurs to the elephant-tamer:
‘Now this forest elephant will surely live,’ [the trainer thinks].
Then the elephant tamer subjects him to further training, saying:
‘Take up, sir! Put down, sir!’
When, Aggivessana, the forest elephant follows the trainer’s instructions regarding taking up and laying down, and carries out his advice, the elephant trainer subjects him to further training:
“Come forward, sir! Go back, sir!
When, Aggivessana, the forest elephant follows the trainer’s instructions regarding coming forward and going back, and carries out his advice, the elephant trainer subjects him to further training:
"Rise up, sir! Sit down, sir!

When, Aggivessana, the forest elephant becomes obedient to the elephant-tamer regarding rising and sitting, and follows his instructions and advice, the elephant-tamer subjects it further to the training known as "immovability" (āneñja) for the sake of its great [strength].
A wooden board is fastened to its trunk; a man with a lance in his hand sits upon its neck,
men with lances in their hands stand surrounding it on all sides, and the elephant trainer stands in front holding a long lance-shaft.
Thus, while performing the immovable feat, he does not move his forefeet nor his hindfeet;
he does not move his forebody nor his hindbody; he does not move his head, nor his ears, nor his tusks, nor his tail, nor his trunk.
Thus the forest elephant becomes one who endures blows from spears, blows from swords, blows from javelins, and blows from arrowheads;

he endures the loud sounds of drums, kettledrums, flutes, conchs, and ḍiṇḍimas. Having eliminated all crookedness and faults and having removed all impurities, he is worthy of a king, an enjoyer of royal wealth, and is reckoned as a very limb of the king.

In the same way, Aggivessana, here a Tathāgata arises in the world, an arahant, a perfectly enlightened one, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
Having realized this world—with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans—by his own direct knowledge, he makes it known.

He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he reveals the holy life (brahmacariya) in its entirety, perfect and pure.
A householder, or a householder’s son, or one born into some other family, hears that Dhamma.
Having heard that Dhamma, he gains faith in the Tathāgata.
Endowed with that attainment of faith, he reflects thus:
"The household life is crowded, a path of dust; going forth is the open air.
It is not easy for one living at home to practice the holy life in its complete perfection, in its complete purity, polished like a conch shell."
‘What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, don saffron robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness?
Then, at a later time, having abandoned a small or large mass of wealth,
and having abandoned a small or large circle of relatives, he shaves off his hair and beard.
Having clothed himself in saffron robes, he goes forth from the household life into homelessness.
To this extent, Aggivessana, a noble disciple has gone out into the open.
For gods and humans, Aggivessana, are greedy for these things: namely, the five strands of sensual pleasure.
The Tathāgata further disciplines him thus:

“Come, bhikkhu, be virtuous; dwell restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and train yourself by undertaking the rules of training.
When, Aggivessana, the noble disciple is virtuous and dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha...
Endowed with proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, he trains himself by undertaking the rules of training.
The Tathāgata further disciplines him thus:
“Come, bhikkhu, be one who guards the doors of the sense faculties. Having seen a form with the eye, do not grasp at its signs … [and so on] …”
(As in the Gaṇaka-Moggallāna Sutta, so should these be elaborated in detail.
Having abandoned these five hindrances— defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom—
he dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings … mind in mind … phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
Just as, Aggivessana, an elephant trainer, having driven a large post into the ground,
binds the neck of a wild forest elephant to it for the purpose of crushing his wild habits,
for the purpose of crushing his wild memories and intentions, and for the purpose of crushing his distress, fatigue, and feverish agitation.

Just so, Aggivessana, for a noble disciple these four foundations of mindfulness serve as a tethering of the mind for the purpose of delighting in the village and for the purpose of establishing others in the virtues dear to human beings;
they serve to crush those virtues based on the household life and to crush those memories and intentions based on the household life.
For the crushing of the distress, fatigue, and fever born of attachment to the household life, for the attainment of the true way, and for the realization of Nibbāna.
Then the Tathāgata further instructs him:
"Come, bhikkhu, dwell contemplating the body as the body, and do not direct your thoughts toward sensual pleasures."
“Dwell contemplating feelings as feelings … the mind as mind … phenomena as phenomena, and do not direct your thoughts toward sensual desires.”

Thus, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and possesses the rapture and happiness born of concentration;
... [he enters] the third jhāna ... [he enters] the fourth jhāna.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it toward the knowledge of recollecting past lives.
He recollects his manifold past lives, that is to say: one birth, two births... [and so on] ...thus with their aspects and particulars, he recollects his manifold past lives.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it toward the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings.

With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—low and high, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it toward the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.
He understands as it really is: "This is suffering"; he understands as it really is: "This is the origin of suffering";
he understands as it really is: "This is the cessation of suffering"; he understands as it really is: "This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering."
He understands it as it really is:
“These are the taints,” he understands as it really is; “This is the origin of the taints,” he understands as it really is;
“This is the cessation of the taints,” he understands as it really is; “This is the practice leading to the cessation of the taints,” he understands as it really is.
One understands it as it truly is.

For one who knows thus and sees thus, the mind is liberated from the influx of sensual desire, the mind is liberated from the influx of existence, and the mind is liberated from the influx of ignorance.
When it is liberated, there arises the knowledge: "It is liberated."
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being’—thus he understands.
That bhikkhu is patient with cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things;
he is patient with abusive and unwelcome modes of speech, and with arisen bodily feelings that are painful...
He is one who is habitually patient with feelings that are painful, harsh, bitter, disagreeable, unpleasant, and life-threatening;

he has removed and eliminated all taints rooted in lust, hatred, and delusion; he is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
Aggivessana, even if an old royal elephant dies untamed and undisciplined, it is reckoned simply as: "An old royal elephant has died an untamed death."

“Aggivessana, even if it is the king’s elephant that is middle-aged, Aggivessana, or even if it is the king’s elephant that is young, yet dies untamed and undisciplined, it is reckoned as ‘the death of one untamed; the young king’s elephant has died.
In the same way, Aggivessana, even if it is an elder bhikkhu who dies with his taints not yet destroyed, he is reckoned as ‘the death of one untamed; the elder bhikkhu has died.’”

“Aggivessana, even if it is a middle-aged monk, Aggivessana, or even if it is a newly ordained monk who dies with his taints not yet destroyed, he is reckoned as: ‘A newly ordained monk has died an undisciplined death.
Aggivessana, even if it is an aged royal elephant that dies—well-tamed and well-trained—it is reckoned as: ‘An aged royal elephant has died a disciplined death.’”

“Aggivessana, even if it is the king’s elephant of middle age… or even if it is the king’s young elephant that dies well-tamed and well-trained, it is reckoned as ‘the death of the tamed; the young king’s elephant has died.
In the same way, Aggivessana, even if it is an elder bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed who dies, he is reckoned as ‘the death of the tamed; the elder bhikkhu has died.’”
“Aggivessana, even if it is a middle-aged bhikkhu,
or even if it is a newly ordained bhikkhu who has exhausted the taints and passes away, he is reckoned as a ‘newly ordained bhikkhu who has passed away with a tamed death.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
The novice Aciravata, glad at heart, rejoiced in the words spoken by the Blessed One.
The fifth discourse, the Dantabhūmi Sutta, is finished.
